AGENDA
  CITY OF ALHAMBRA
  TRANSPORTATION COMMISSION
  REGULAR MEETING

  January 8, 2020  7:00 pm  Conference Room A, Alhambra City Hall

1. Call to Order

2. Roll Call

  Lucy Banuelos  Cliff Bender
  Antonio Chavira Jr.  Gwen Chen
  Lilian De Loza Gutierrez  Albert Lu
  Kaysa Moreno  Steven Placido

3. Approval of the Minutes of September 11, 2019

4. Traffic Safety Review of the Intersections of Palmetto Drive and 2nd Street and Linda
  Vista Avenue at 2nd Street

  Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a citizen request for the installation
  of an all-way stop control at the intersection of Palmetto and 2nd and at Linda Vista and
  Palmetto Avenue.

  The study concluded that the intersections at 2nd Street and Palmetto Drive and at 2nd Street
  and Linda Vista Avenue did not meet warrants for the installation of all-way stop control.

  Recommended Action

  It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City
  Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
  measures outlined in the report.

5. Traffic Safety Review of Intersection of 5th and Commonwealth Avenue

  Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a citizen request for the installation
  of an all-way stop control at the intersection of 5th and Commonwealth Avenue.

  The study finds that an all-way stop control is not warranted at this location and recommends
  the installation of additional signage and truncated domes for ADA compliance on the curb
  ramps.

  Recommended Action

  It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City
  Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
  measures outlined in the report.

  1
 6. Traffic Safety Review of Westmont Drive between Concord Avenue and Poplar
  Boulevard

  Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a citizen request for traffic calming
  measures on Westmont Drive between Concord Avenue and Poplar Boulevard.

  As a result of extensive field data collection and review, the study concluded that vehicles are
  traveling within the posted speed limit of 25 MPH.

  The intersection of Westmont Drive at Norwich Avenue was studied separately to check if it
  met warrants for an all-way stop since it is the only intersection in the segment that has two-
  way stop control in the east and west directions, all other intersections are all-way stop
  controlled. The intersection did not meet warrants for an all-way stop per the California Manual
  of Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA-MUTCD) and the California Vehicle Code (CVC).

  To reinforce the speed limit on Westmont Avenue it is recommended to install additional speed
  limit signs and “25” pavement legends. Placement of official traffic control devices on public
  streets is guided by the California Manual of Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CA-MUTCD)
  and the California Vehicle Code (CVC).

  Recommended Action

  It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City
  Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
  measures outlined in the report.

7. Traffic Safety Review of the intersection of 9th Street and Norwood Place

  Staff will review the report that was prepared in response to a citizen request for the installation
  of an all-way stop control at the intersection of 9th and Norwood Place.

  The study finds that an all-way stop control is not warranted at this location and recommends
  the installation of additional red curb to improve line of sight and the installation of “Cross
  Traffic Does Not Stop” signage for eastbound and westbound traffic, under existing STOP
  signs.

  Recommended Action

  It is recommended that the Transportation Commission review the report with the City
  Engineer, listen to public comment and authorize staff to implement the additional safety
  measures outlined in the report.

8. Public Comments

  Comments must pertain to the business of the Transportation Commission. Kindly limit all
  oral communications to five (5) minutes.

9. Comments and concerns from Commission Members and/or Staff.

  Comments, concerns or discussion on any item(s) not specified on the agenda. Items
  discussed must pertain to the business of the Alhambra Transportation Commission.

  2
 10. Adjournment

  Adjournment to a regular meeting on Wednesday, March 11, 2020 at 7:00 p.m.

Copies of staff reports or other written documentation, if any, relating to each item of business
described above are on file in the Alhambra City Hall, Public Works Department, 111 S. First
Street, Alhambra California 91801 and are available for public inspection upon request during
regular business hours of 7:00am to 5:30pm, Monday through Thursday.

Should any person have a question concerning any of the above agenda items prior to the
meeting described herein, he or she may contact Martin Ray, Director of Public Works & Utilities,
either in person at the Public Works Department at Alhambra City Hall, 111 South First Street, or
by calling via telephone at (626) 570-5067 during regular business hours.

  Traffic Engineer Jana Robbins reviewed with the Commission the traffic

  The study finds that replacement signage, restriping of the crosswalks, ADA

  Resident Oscar Francia spoke of his concerns regarding the intersection of
  Almansor and Los Higos as to both the vehicle and pedestrian traffic with the
  school and park being in such close proximity. It was explained by the Traffic
  Engineer Jana Robbins that the intersection does not meet the MUTCD
  warrants for the installation of a traffic signal.

  Commission Placido explained that if the recommended improvements of the
  study were passed by the Commission, he hoped it would improve traffic
  movement in the area. Commissioner Bender commended Mr. Francia for his
  efforts to improve traffic in the area.

  Traffic Engineer Jana Robbins reviewed the report that was prepared in

  Las Flores turning movement could be looked at. Due to the street width

CRITERIA FOR DETERMINING IF STOP CONTROL IS WARRANTED
Traffic control devices work in concert with the basic “rules of the road” contained in traffic laws and
ordinances. The California Manual of Uniform Traffic Devices (CAMUTCD Section 2B.07) describes
applications, warrants, and placement of STOP signs (R1-1). The STOP sign is a regulatory device that is
used when traffic is required to stop. STOP signs are used to assign right-of-way at an intersection. Multi-
way control is used where the volume of traffic on the intersecting roads is approximately equal.

Stop signs are not used as a speed control device. Since a STOP sign causes inconvenience to motorists, it
should be used only where warranted. The placement of these signs is dictated by engineering judgment
and based on guidelines found in the CAMUTCD and CVC. The City’s criteria for determining if two-way
or all-way stop control is warranted is based on several factors as set by the CAMUTCD. These factors
include minimum volume on each of the street approaches, accident investigation, speed of traffic,
number of pedestrians and potential sight obstructions.

All-Way Stop Installation

The following briefly outlines the Criteria for the installation of All-Way stop warrants.

ALL-WAY STOP CONTROL WARRANTS FOR INSTALLATION (LINDA VISTA AVENUE AND SECOND STREET)

The placement of All-Way stop control is warranted when:
  A. Traffic control signals are justified
  B. A crash problem exists as indicated by 5 or more accidents in a 12-month period
  C. Minimum Volumes are met if:
  1. Volume entering intersection from the major approach (total of both approaches)
  averages 300 vehicles per hour for any 8 hours of an average day.
  2. The combined vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle volumes entering the intersection from the
  minor street approaches averages at least 200 units per hour for the same 8 hours.
  If the 85th percentile approach speed of the major street exceeds 40 mph, the minimum
  volumes are 70 percent of the above values.

As a part of this study, a review of the intersections of 2nd Street at Palmetto Drive and at 2nd Street at
Linda Vista Avenue was conducted. Based on the analysis and field review conducted it was determined
that neither of the intersections met the warrants for the installation of All-Way STOP control.

LINE OF SIGHT AT INTERSECTIONS
The driver of a vehicle approaching or departing from an intersection should have an unobstructed view
of the intersection, including any traffic control devices, and enough lengths along the intersecting
highway to permit the driver to anticipate and avoid potential collisions (Maze and Plazak 2000). These
unobstructed views form triangular areas known as sight triangles. Any object within the sight triangle
that would obstruct the driver’s view of an approaching vehicle should be removed or modified or
appropriate traffic control devices should be installed as per the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control
Devices. Obstructions within sight triangles could be buildings, vehicles, hedges, trees, bushes, tall crops,
walls, fences or parked cars. A parked vehicle extends approximately 7-feet to 8-feet from the curb, so it’s
necessary to consider the width of a vehicle when determining the amount of red curb needed to obtain
a clear sight triangle (See Figures 11-16). The line of sight uses the driver’s eye height for measurement
(3’ 6”).

  Per AASHTO’s guidelines, for a roadway with a posted
  speed of 25 mph the sight distance is 155 feet.

RECOMMENDATIONS

The study concluded that the intersections at 2nd Street and Palmetto Drive and at 2nd Street and Linda
Vista Avenue did not meet warrants for the installation of all-way stop control. However, the following
measures will increase line of sight for waiting vehicles at each intersection as well as remind drivers that
traffic does not stop in the east and west directions at the 2nd Street and Palmetto Drive intersection and
in the north and south directions at the 2nd Street and Linda Vista Avenue. The following recommendations
have been provided:

  1. Install four (4) “CROSS TRAFFIC DOES NOT STOP” signs (W4-4P). Per Figure 17, signs are to be
  installed at the stop-controlled legs of each intersection.
  • One sign for eastbound traffic at 2nd Street and Palmetto Drive
  • One sign for westbound traffic at 2nd Street and Palmetto Drive
  • One sign for northbound traffic at 2nd Street and Linda Vista Avenue
  • One sign for southbound traffic at 2nd Street and Linda Vista Avenue

  2. Install red curb along Palmetto Drive on the north and south sides at its intersection with 2nd Street
  and repaint the existing red curb at the intersection of 2nd Street and Linda Vista Avenue per Figure
  17. (Figure 3B-21 CAMUTCD)

CRITERIA FOR DETERMINING IF STOP CONTROL IS WARRANTED

Traffic control devices work in concert with the basic “rules of the road” contained in traffic laws and
ordinances. The California Manual of Uniform Traffic Devices (CAMUTCD Section 2B.07) describes
applications, warrants, and placement of STOP signs (R1-1). The STOP sign is a regulatory device that is
used when traffic is required to stop. STOP signs are used to assign right-of-way at an intersection. Multi-
way control is used where the volume of traffic on the intersecting roads is approximately equal.

Stop signs are not used as a speed control device. Since a STOP sign causes inconvenience to motorists, it
should be used only where warranted. The City’s criteria for determining if two-way or all-way stop
control is warranted is based on a number of factors as set by the CAMUTCD. These factors include
minimum volume on each of the street approaches, accident investigation, speed of traffic, number of
pedestrians and potential sight obstructions.

ALL-WAY STOP CONTROL WARRANTS FOR INSTALLATION

The placement of All-Way stop control is warranted when:
  A. Traffic control signals are justified (Not Met)
  B. A crash problem exists as indicated by 5 or more accidents in a 12-month period (Not Met)
  C. Minimum Volumes are met if:
  1. Volume entering intersection from the major approach (total of both approaches)
  averages 300 vehicles per hour for any 8 hours of an average day. (Met) And
  2. The combined vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle volumes entering the intersection from the
  minor street approaches averages at least 200 units per hour for the same 8 hours. (Not
  Met)
  3. If the 85th percentile approach speed of the major-street exceeds 40 mph, the minimum
  volumes are 70 percent of the above values. (Not Met)

RECOMMENDATIONS

The study concluded that the intersection did not meet warrants for the installation of all way stop at the
intersection of 5th Street and Commonwealth Avenue as determined by the California Manual of Uniform
Traffic Control Devices (CAMUTCD). A stop sign is an inconvenience to motorists, because of this, stop
signs should only be placed if they meet a CAMUTCD warrant. Stop signs are frequently violated if
unwarranted. There are existing stop signs at the intersections, approximately 370-feet, east and west of
the 5th Street and Commonwealth Avenue intersection.

It is recommended to repaint the existing red curbs which help to improve the safety of vehicles exiting
from 5th Street by increasing their line of sight. Also, speed can be mitigated by the installation of speed
limit signs at the points of entry from the major streets nearby.

A summary of recommendations at the intersection of 5th Street and Commonwealth Avenue are as
follows:
  1. Install truncated domes on the all of the corners at Commonwealth Avenue and 5th Avenue. To
  meet ADA requirements.

  2. Repaint existing red curb at each current location as shown in Figures 13 and 14.

  3. Work with Alhambra Police Department to do random spot speed enforcement and place their

CRITERIA FOR DETERMINING IF STOP CONTROL IS WARRANTED

Traffic control devices work in concert with the basic “rules of the road” contained in traffic laws and
ordinances. The California Manual of Uniform Traffic Control Devices (CAMUTCD) describes applications,
warrants, and placement of STOP signs (R1-1). The STOP sign is a regulatory device that is used when
traffic is required to stop. STOP signs are used to assign right-of-way at an intersection. Multi-way control
is used where the volume of traffic on the intersecting roads is approximately equal. Stop signs are not
used as a speed control device.

Since a STOP sign causes inconvenience to motorists, it should be used only where warranted. The City’s
criteria for determining if two-way or all-way stop control is warranted is based on several factors as set
by the CAMUTCD. These factors include minimum volumes on each of the street approaches, accident
investigation, speed of traffic, number of pedestrians and potential sight obstructions.

All-Way Stop Installation

The following briefly outlines the Criteria for the installation of All-Way Stop at the intersection of
Westmont Drive and Norwich Avenue.

The placement of All-Way stop control is warranted when1:

A. Traffic control signals are justified (not met)
B. A crash problem exists as indicated by 5 or more accidents in a 12-month period (not met)
C. Minimum Volumes are met if:
  1. Volume entering intersection from the major approach (total of both approaches) averages
  300 vehicles per hour for any 8 hours of an average day. (not met) And
  2. The combined vehicle, pedestrian and bicycle volumes entering the intersection from the
  minor street approaches averages at least 200 units per hour for the same 8 hours. (not met)
  3. If the 85th percentile approach speed of the major street exceeds 40 mph the minimum
  volumes are 70 percent of the above values. (not met)

LINE OF SIGHT AT INTERSECTIONS

Improving Line of Sight for Vehicles Entering an Intersection: At side street crossings, generous sight
distances and unobstructed sight lines allow motorists and pedestrians to detect each other in time to
avoid collisions. At side streets providing a clear corner line of sight allows a motorist pulling into through
traffic to observe and accurately determine the approaching vehicles speed to safely maneuver into
traffic.

If a motorist has only a brief glimpse of a waiting pedestrian or car, he or she may not sufficiently slow his
or her approach to the side street and not anticipate a crossing vehicle in time to stop. A vehicle’s driver
needs to be able to have room to stop before colliding with something in the roadway, such as a a stopped
vehicle or road debris. To allow drivers to perceive, react, and safely stop, a minimum stopping sight
distance must be available. Stopping sight distance is defined as the sum of two distances (AASHTO, Green
Book):

  1. Reaction distance—the distance traveled by the vehicle from the instant the driver sees an object
  necessitating a stop to the instant the brakes are applied; plus
  2. Braking distance—the distance traveled by the vehicle from the instant brake application begins
  to the instant when the vehicle has come to complete stop.

INTRODUCTION/BACKGROUND

On behalf of the City of Alhambra, Transtech Engineers Inc. has completed a traffic review to evaluate a
resident request for all-way stop control at the intersection of 9th Street and Norwood Place. The resident
who submitted the request and resides near the intersection stated that they are concerned with the
safety of everyone in the surrounding area. The resident claims there are accidents at the intersection
monthly and potential accidents daily with some collisions resulting in vehicles on the lawn of nearby
properties. As part of this traffic assessment, a review of existing roadway conditions, 6 years of collision
data, daily traffic counts, a radar speed sample as well as peak hour vehicular and pedestrian counts were
completed.

EXISTING CONDITIONS

9th Street (ADT: 2,794 – November 12, 2019): 9th Street is a 30’ (feet) wide local road that runs north/south

on 9th Street is to the north at Valley Boulevard where there is a traffic signal and to the south at Glendon
Way where there is an all-way stop. Parking is prohibited on Fridays from 12:00PM to 3:00PM on the east
side of 9th Street and on Fridays from 8:00AM to 11:30AM on the west side of 9th Street due to street
sweeping restrictions.

Norwood Place (ADT: 1,268 – November 12, 2019): Norwood Place runs east/west and is considered a
collector street in Alhambra’s General Plan. Norwood Place is approximately 28’ (feet) wide, with no
center line and one travel lane in each direction with a posted speed limit of 25 MPH. Parking is allowed
on both sides of the street. Norwood Place at 9th Street is stop controlled in the east and west directions.
The nearest traffic control west of the intersection is at Atlantic Boulevard where there is a stop sign for
eastbound and westbound traffic and to east of the intersection at 6th Street where there is an all-way
stop. Parking is prohibited on Fridays from 12:00PM to 3:00PM on the north side of Norwood Place and
on Fridays from 8:00AM to 11:30AM on the south side of Norwood Place due to street sweeping
restrictions.

CRITERIA FOR DETERMINING IF STOP CONTROL IS WARRANTED
Traffic control devices work in concert with the basic “rules of the road” contained in traffic laws and
ordinances. The California Manual of Uniform Traffic Devices (CAMUTCD Section 2B.07) describes
applications, warrants, and placement of STOP signs (R1-1). The STOP sign is a regulatory device that is
used when traffic is required to stop. STOP signs are used to assign right-of-way at an intersection. Multi-
way control is used where the volume of traffic on the intersecting roads is approximately equal.

Stop signs are not used as a speed control device. Since a STOP sign causes inconvenience to motorists, it
should be used only where warranted. The City’s criteria for determining if two-way or all-way stop control
is warranted is based on a number of factors as set by the CAMUTCD. These factors include minimum
volume on each of the street approaches, accident investigation, speed of traffic, number of pedestrians
and potential sight obstructions.

All-Way Stop Installation

The following briefly outlines the Criteria for the installation of All-Way stop warrants as found in Section
2B.07 of the CAMUTCD.

ALL-WAY STOP CONTROL WARRANTS FOR INSTALLATION

The placement of All-Way stop control is warranted when:
  A. Traffic control signals are justified (Not Met)
  B. A crash problem exists as indicated by 5 or more accidents in a 12-month period (Not Met)
  C. Minimum Volumes are met if:
  1. Volume entering intersection from the major street approaches (total of both
  approaches) averages 300 vehicles per hour for any 8 hours of an average day. (Not Met-
  under 300)
  2. The combined vehicle, pedestrian, and bicycle volume entering the intersection from the
  minor street approaches (total of both approaches) averages at least 200 units per hour
  for the same 8 hours. (Not Met- under 200)
  3. If the 85th percentile approach speed of the major-street exceeds 40 mph, the minimum
  volumes are 70 percent of the above values.

LINE OF SIGHT AT INTERSECTIONS

The driver of a vehicle approaching or departing from an intersection should have an unobstructed view
of the intersection, including any traffic control devices, and sufficient lengths along the intersecting
highway to permit the driver to anticipate and avoid potential collisions (Maze and Plazak 2000). These
unobstructed views form triangular areas known as sight triangles. Any object within the sight triangle
that would obstruct the driver’s view of an approaching vehicle should be removed or modified or
appropriate traffic control devices should be installed as per the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control
Devices. Obstructions within sight triangles could be buildings, vehicles, hedges, trees, bushes, tall crops,
walls, fences or parked cars. A parked vehicle extends approximately 7-feet from the curb, so it’s
necessary to take into account the width of a vehicle when determining the amount of red curb needed
to obtain a clear sight triangle (Figure 9 and 10). The line of sight uses the driver’s eye height for
measurement (3’ 6”).

  Per AASHTO’s guidelines, for a roadway with a posted
  speed of 25 mph the sight distance is 155 feet.

RECOMMENDATIONS

The study concluded that the intersection did not meet warrants for the installation of all way stop at the
intersection of 9th Street and Norwood Place as determined by the California Manual of Uniform Traffic
Control Devices (CAMUTCD). A stop sign is an inconvenience to motorists, because of this, stop signs
should only be placed if they meet a CAMUTCD warrant. Stop signs are frequently violated if unwarranted.
However, the following measures will increase line of sight for vehicles waiting to make a right/left turn
